docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. VOGON helps and gets out of the way. It does not impose heavy workflows or bureaucracy.
  2. The process comes from the host project's validation plan, not from VOGON.
  3. A skipped or late step is reported, never blocked.
  4. VOGON never approves or signs. People do.
  5. Evidence never comes from a model.
  6. All work is reviewed by a different agent.

The writing standard is the plugin's src/vogon/references/writing.md.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
VOGON is a Claude Code plugin installed into a host project: the repository of a regulated (GxP) software project. It carries out the steps of the GxP process that do not need a person. The plugin is a set of skills, the sub-agents they start, and the commands vogon id, vogon approve and vogon trace for the work that must give the same result every time. Claude Code does all model work, and the Python code calls no language model (DEC-005).

src/vogon/references/common.md holds the rules every skill applies and lists the topic file in src/vogon/references/ that holds each other rule. Each skill's steps are in src/vogon/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md. Sub-agents do the work in their own contexts, so the main agent's context stays small over a long task. A different sub-agent reviews each piece (principle 6, common.md "Sub-agents"). Vocabulary defines the terms, and Records describes the files under vogon/, including the state file.

docs.title: Scope and systems
docs.text:
Version 0.1 is developed and tested against one stack: a host project in Python with pytest, GitHub as repository host, Jira as tracker, Xray as test manager, and Claude Code. No abstraction layer is written before a second implementation exists (DEC-004).

The host project's validation plan chooses its products, so a skill names each external system by its role: repository host, tracker, test manager, document system, meetings, mail and chat (common.md "Systems by role").

VOGON never moves an item into a state that records approval or signature, because a signature requires the signer's own credentials (CON-001). common.md "Actions VOGON never takes" lists these actions and their exceptions. An approval recorded by vogon approve carries the approver's git identity and asks for no credentials, so it is not an electronic signature under 21 CFR Part 11.

A change to a live system is recorded and approved in the host project's own change control system. VOGON writes no change record and no impact assessment, and the change's requirements, tests, code and release documents go through the same skills as the first release (DEC-026).

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
One skill per task a person starts. Each runs in the main Claude Code session.

# Step Skill Produces Approved by 1 Configure vogon:init vogon/project/vogon.yaml, the validation plan in vogon/sources/, the .gitignore lines, the conftest.py lines and the marker registration A person, on the pull request 2 File the sources vogon:requirements Reviewed summaries of meetings, mail and chat; filed documents with their markdown copies 3 Draft and review the records vogon:requirements Requirements with acceptance criteria and risk fields; facts, constraints and decisions; withdrawals and supersessions 4 Send the requirements for approval vogon:requirements The pull request with REQ-*.md and REQ-*.json; tracker items where a tracker is configured 5 Approve the requirements vogon:approve, or the tracker An approved entry in REQ-*.json, or the tracker's approval transition where a tracker holds approvals The requirement approver 6 Write the test procedures vogon:tests Test procedures, where tests.md requires them The roles tests.md names 7 Choose a requirement vogon:next The ready and not-ready lists; the tracker item assigned 8 Plan vogon:implement A reviewed plan, and a planned entry A developer, when asked 9 Write the code, tests and documentation vogon:implement Reviewed code, tests and documentation, all tests passing, in one pull request A person, on the repository host 10 Release vogon:release The documents documents.md lists, the traceability matrix and the results, filed The roles documents.md names

Different requirements are at different steps at the same time. Step 6 comes before step 7 or after step 9, as tests.md states; a project that needs no test procedures skips it. A change to a requirement after step 4 appends a changed entry and returns the requirement to step 5.

The default checklists are in the references/ directory of the requirements and implement skills. Each is a separate file so that a project can replace one with a file of the same name in vogon/project/checklists/ (common.md "Sub-agents").

docs.title: Start of a skill
docs.text: Tasks happen weeks apart, by different developers, in any order, so a skill does not assume an earlier task ran (common.md "Start of every skill").

docs.title: Project configuration and process files
docs.text:
vogon/project/vogon.yaml names the system for each role, the holders of each approval role and the modules. vogon:init writes it from src/vogon/templates/vogon.yaml. It is YAML because the commands read it.

The validation plan is filed in vogon/sources/ as the original and a markdown copy (Sources). It stays the host project's controlled document, and VOGON never edits either copy. The process files in vogon/project/ are VOGON's reading of the plan: tracking.md, requirements.md, tests.md, traceability.md, documents.md and release.md. Their topics are in their templates in src/vogon/templates/.

docs.title: Sources and records
docs.text: Records are markdown files under vogon/ in the host repository (Records), drafted from held documents and reviewed summaries (Sources). A requirement whose only source is code describes current behaviour, defects included, so the developer confirms that the behaviour is intended (src/vogon/skills/requirements/SKILL.md, step 5).

docs.title: Requirement lifecycle
docs.text:
The rules for approval, change, withdrawal and supersession are in src/vogon/references/lifecycle.md.

The requirement approver is the role named in the "Approval" section of requirements.md, because the validation plan sets who approves (principle 2). When that section names no role, it is the Product Owner.

A requirement is approved in one of two places: in the tracker, where tracking.md states an approval transition for the requirement item type, and otherwise in the state file, by vogon approve.

On a withdrawal or a supersession, vogon:requirements reports the tests, procedures, plans and records that name the old id and changes none of them, because changing them is work for vogon:implement and vogon:tests.

docs.title: Risk
docs.text: Each requirement carries gxp_impact and risk, each with its reason, from the moment it is drafted, so a reader can challenge a value. The default values and method are in src/vogon/references/records.md "Requirement", and requirements.md replaces them where the validation plan states its own. Project-level risk documents the plan lists, such as a risk log or a data integrity risk assessment, are separate documents, approved by the roles the plan names.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The pytest code is the test case. Each test names the requirements it verifies in @pytest.mark.req, and where procedures exist, its procedures in @pytest.mark.procedure. The link is on the test because whoever changes a test edits its marker in the same edit (DEC-006). The marker rules are in src/vogon/references/markers.md. A test with no req marker is allowed and verifies no requirement in the matrix.

An expected value is worked out from the requirement and its sources, because a value read off the code makes the test that asserts it unable to fail (records.md "Expected values").

docs.title: Code from requirements
docs.text: vogon:implement writes a plan, vogon/plans/plan_<slug>.md, that divides the work into parts. Each part is written by its own sub-agent and reviewed against the test checklist and by Claude Code's code-review skill. VOGON has no code reviewer of its own.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
vogon:init adds lines to the host conftest.py that copy each test's req and procedure marker ids into the JUnit XML properties (markers.md). tests.md states how a test run is tied to the commit it tested. By default the suite name is the full commit hash. A pytest run that names the suite this way is:

pytest --junitxml=results.xml -o junit_suite_name=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

Where a test manager is configured, VOGON uploads the JUnit XML unchanged and the test manager produces the traceability report, because it is a tool with its own validation (DEC-003). Where none is configured, vogon trace joins the markers and results of one commit into the matrix, including every requirement with no test. The matrix is evidence, so it comes from the test manager or from vogon trace, never from a model (principle 5).

docs.title: Release
docs.text: vogon:release takes a release commit, a release name and the JUnit XML of a test run on that commit. Sub-agents draft each document documents.md lists from a read-only checkout of that commit, so every statement describes the code released. The steps are in src/vogon/skills/release/SKILL.md.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path Contents .claude-plugin/ The marketplace listing. src/vogon/ The Claude Code plugin: skills, references, templates. src/docs/ Documentation source, markdown. src/html/ Marketing page source: index.html, img/. docs/ Build output. Rendered HTML, served by GitHub Pages. Never edit. vogon/ VOGON's own constraints and decisions, in the record format of Records. tmp/ Working notes and plans. Gitignored, local only. assets/ Brand originals. Never published. .githooks/ The pre-commit hook that rebuilds docs/.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
uv sync
git config core.hooksPath .githooks

pyproject.toml exists for development only: it holds the dev dependency group.

docs.title: Building the site
docs.text:
make site     # src/docs/ -> docs/, then src/html/ copied over the top
make serve    # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000
make clean    # rm -rf docs/

docs/ is committed because Pages serves it from git. .githooks/pre-commit rebuilds and stages it when a commit touches src/docs/, src/html/ or mkdocs.yml. A failed build aborts the commit, and --strict makes a broken link fail it.

mkdocs and mkdocs-material are in the dev dependency group, run through uv run --group dev, and uv.lock fixes their versions. uvx mkdocs is not used: it resolves a fresh version each time, and the rendered output is committed.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
GitHub Pages, deploy from a branch: Settings → Pages → Source "Deploy from a branch", branch main, folder /docs.

src/html/index.html            → /
src/html/img/emblem.webp       → /img/emblem.webp
src/docs/user/install.md       → /user/install.html
src/docs/dev/architecture.md   → /dev/architecture.html
assets/                        → not served

src/html/.nojekyll copies through to docs/.nojekyll and stops GitHub re-running Jekyll over HTML that mkdocs already rendered. mkdocs-material writes its theme CSS and JS into docs/assets/, which is unrelated to the top-level assets/.

docs.title: The plugin
docs.text:
The repository is a Claude Code plugin marketplace. .claude-plugin/marketplace.json lists the plugin vogon, with source ./src/vogon:

src/vogon/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   name, version, description
├── references/                  rules shared by the skills, one file per topic
├── templates/                   templates of vogon.yaml and the process files
└── skills/
    ├── init/                    SKILL.md
    ├── requirements/            SKILL.md, references/
    ├── approve/                 SKILL.md
    ├── next/                    SKILL.md
    ├── tests/                   SKILL.md
    ├── implement/               SKILL.md, references/
    └── release/                 SKILL.md

The version is in plugin.json and nowhere else. There is no wheel and no PyPI release.

Each release is tagged v<version>, with the version read from plugin.json, on the commit that sets it: v0.1.0 for version 0.1.0.

claude plugin validate .           # the marketplace listing
claude plugin validate src/vogon   # the plugin manifest

To test the plugin as a host project sees it, open Claude Code in a scratch git repository and run:

/plugin marketplace add /path/to/repo --scope project
/plugin install vogon@vogon --scope project

Claude Code copies the plugin into its cache at install, keyed by version. A change in the working tree reaches the scratch repository only after the plugin is uninstalled and installed again; /plugin update does nothing while the version is unchanged.

docs.title: Records
docs.text: Vocabulary defines the four kinds of record. The rules for every record, including ids, paths, frontmatter fields and body blocks, are in src/vogon/references/records.md. Every record also follows src/vogon/references/writing.md.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
VOGON creates this layout under vogon/ in a host project. This repository's vogon/ holds VOGON's own constraints and decisions in the same format.

Path Holds vogon/project/ vogon.yaml and the process files derived from the validation plan (src/vogon/references/process-files.md); checklists/ holds the project's own versions of the default checklists vogon/requirements/<module>/ Requirements REQ-*.md, each with its state file REQ-*.json beside it, and the test procedures kept in the repository. A project without modules uses vogon/requirements/ vogon/facts/ Domain facts vogon/constraints/ Constraints vogon/decisions/ Decisions vogon/sources/ Held copies of the documents records cite (Sources) vogon/plans/ Plans for code; done/ holds the plans whose requirements have all been released vogon/documents/<release>/ Drafted documents for one release, where the project has no document system vogon/tmp/ Working files, such as downloaded transcripts and draft documents. Gitignored

Requirements are grouped by module. Facts, constraints and decisions are flat, because one is often cited by several modules.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
YAML frontmatter is read by the skills and the commands, and the markdown body by people. Approval is not a field and not a status: src/vogon/references/lifecycle.md "Approval" states where an approval is recorded.

source lists the held documents a record came from. Each path in it asserts that the document says what the record says, so only a passage that was read is cited.

status records whether the project is committed to the statement. Build progress is in the state file and the passing tests.

docs.title: Requirement
docs.text:
---
id: REQ-PRN-12
type: requirement
title: Print the sample id as a barcode on the tube label
modules: [PRN]
status: active
source:
  - vogon/sources/2026-09-15_sample_labelling.summary.md
verification: test
gxp_impact: data integrity
gxp_impact_reason: A wrong barcode attaches a result to the wrong sample.
risk: high
risk_reason: A mismatch harms the sample record, occurs whenever a label is
  reprinted from stale data, and is not visible to the person applying it.
---

# REQ-PRN-12: Print the sample id as a barcode on the tube label

**Requirement.** The label printer MUST encode the sample id stored for the
tube, and only that id, in a Code 128 barcode on its label.

**Out of scope.** The label layout, and printing labels for anything other
than sample tubes.

**Example.** Sample S-2026-00417 is registered. Its tube label carries a
barcode that a scanner reads as `S-2026-00417`.

**Acceptance criteria.**

- The barcode on a printed label decodes to the stored sample id.
- A label reprinted after the sample id was corrected decodes to the
  corrected id.
- A sample with no stored id produces no label and an error.

docs.title: State file
docs.text:
Each requirement has a state file beside its markdown file, named for the same id with .json. It records every step done to the requirement, in order. The entries and their fields are defined in lifecycle.md "State file".

When an entry and the pull request, commit or tracker item it names differ, the linked item is correct. For approvals, lifecycle.md "Approval" states which record holds them (src/vogon/references/common.md "Start of every skill").

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
A file is named for its id alone, such as REQ-PRN-12.md, so that a changed title breaks no link. A record's history is its git history.

vogon id takes the next number from every branch and the history. Two branches can take the same id before either pushes, so a skill runs vogon id --check and renumbers before it opens its pull request (common.md "Commands").

docs.title: Marketing page
docs.text: src/html/index.html is standalone: no build step, copied verbatim into docs/ by make site. It reads as an enterprise life-sciences SaaS page that is also a controlled document. It has a persistent document-control strip, SOP clause numbering (§1.0 …), square-cornered hairline panels, and two animations that run together when a change request is submitted: the REJECTED stamp lands (slam) and its card shakes (shk). Both are off under prefers-reduced-motion.

docs.title: Type and color
docs.text:
Archivo for display, Source Sans 3 for body, IBM Plex Mono for document metadata and CLI, Source Serif 4 italic for quotes.

Color tokens are sampled from the artwork: paper #FBFAF5, ink #101820, oxblood #971A1C, stamp #BF100F, slate #6E7B82, rule #DFDACF. Light and dark are both defined on :root. Fixed dark chrome (nav strip, footer, consent bar) uses the --dark-ground* tokens and stays dark in both themes.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Images are WebP in src/html/img/, referenced relatively as img/… so the paths survive the copy into docs/. Regenerate with ImageMagick from assets/images/ after adding artwork.

Most of the artwork was drawn on white paper, which glares on a dark page, so those figures have a dark twin, assets/images/<name>_dark.png, served as src/html/img/<name>_dark.webp where one exists. 03 and 08 are served dark as emblem_dark.webp and stamp-alpha_dark.webp. The twins were redrawn for dark ground; flood fills and lightness inversions were tried and rejected.

A dark twin must be the same pixel size as the light .webp beside it, because index.html carries one width/height pair for both sources:

magick identify -format '%wx%h' src/html/img/<name>.webp
magick assets/images/<name>_dark.png -resize '<W>x<H>!' \
  -quality 82 -define webp:method=6 src/html/img/<name>_dark.webp

Where the aspect ratios differ, as for 04, which is square in dark and 1200×1006 in light, centre-crop to the light ratio first (-gravity center -crop 1254x1051+0+0 +repage) rather than squashing.

emblem.webp (03) and stamp-alpha.webp (08) are transparent cutouts and both are white-keyed: the vogon's white shirt and the paper inside the stamp frame went with the background. That reads correctly on cream and leaves holes on dark ground. Their dark counterparts are made from the authored dark artwork: emblem_dark.webp is a circular mask of 03-vogon-icon_dark.png, and stamp-alpha_dark.webp takes its alpha from the brightest channel of 08-rejected-stamp_dark.png. The footer stamp uses the dark one unconditionally because the footer is --dark-ground in both themes. The rejection dialog keeps stamp-alpha.webp, which is the stronger red on its cream card.

A figure with a dark twin is served through <picture> with media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)", in index.html and in the README. There is no theme toggle, so the media query is the only mechanism that switches images. The CSS also has :root[data-theme="dark"] and :not([data-theme="light"]) rules, but nothing sets data-theme, so only the prefers-color-scheme branch takes effect.

docs.title: Lightbox
docs.text:
Every figure is click-to-enlarge. Wrap it in <div class="zoomfig" role="button" tabindex="0"> and the lightbox picks it up, captioned from the image's data-ref. The footer REJECTED stamp is one of these.

The lightbox fits a figure whole and never enlarges it past its own pixels. Portrait figures are the exception: VGN-PROC-001 is a tall chart containing body text, and fitted to the dialog height it is unreadable. A figure taller than it is wide is sized to the dialog width instead, capped at 1.5× its own pixels, and the area scrolls. Clicking the figure does not close the dialog; only the backdrop does.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: A record cites the documents it came from, and those documents are held in vogon/sources/ so that the citation can be checked years later. The filing rules are in src/vogon/references/sources.md.

docs.title: Location and name
docs.text:
The directory is flat. A document's kind is in its frontmatter, not its directory, because a record cites a meeting summary and a standard the same way.

vogon/sources/2026-09-17_requirements_workshop.summary.md
vogon/sources/2026-04-02_electronic_records_procedure.pdf
vogon/sources/2026-04-02_electronic_records_procedure.md

The date in the name is the document's own, such as the meeting day or the issue date, so the directory sorts chronologically and two versions differ by name.

docs.title: Original and markdown copy
docs.text:
A document that is not already markdown is held as the original and a markdown copy. The original is the evidence. The markdown copy can be diffed and searched, and a reviewer sees in a pull request what a record was written from. A copy is never corrected by hand, because a hand-edited copy no longer says what the original says and nothing shows it.

A held document is never changed after filing. A citation asserts that a specific document says something, and a document edited after the fact cannot support that.

docs.title: Meetings, mail and chat
docs.text:
A meeting, mail thread or chat channel is held only as a reviewed summary. A transcript holds personal remarks and discussion unrelated to the project, and the meeting system keeps it under its own retention rule. The downloaded transcript and messages are therefore kept in the gitignored vogon/tmp/ and deleted before the skill commits.

The summary is reviewed against the download before the download is deleted, because a statement the source did not make cannot be found afterwards. A requirement drafted from a summary is binding once the requirement approver approves it; the meeting is only where it came from.

docs.title: Authority
docs.text: authority states how strong a document is, from regulation to informal. It decides what a record may claim from the document, and a source list is ordered by it. The table of what each value may support is in src/vogon/references/sources.md "Authority".

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Projects often keep four kinds of statement in one requirements list under one numbering. Most of those rows cannot be tested. VOGON keeps them as four kinds of record.

docs.title: The two projects
docs.text:
VOGON is one codebase installed into another, so the two are named apart.

VOGON project: this repository. VOGON's own code and documentation, and its constraints and decisions in vogon/.

Host project: a project VOGON is installed into, holding that project's own code, tests and records. User project means the same thing; host project is the term used in the documentation.

docs.title: The four kinds of record
docs.text:
Everything written down that the system will be built from is one of four kinds of record. Each has its own id namespace and its own file (Records). Test procedures are records too, with the id prefix TP, but they describe how a requirement is verified and are defined under Tests below.

Requirement: something the system must do. Written as a MUST statement saying what has to be true and not how, so that a test could fail it. Ids are REQ-<MODULE>-<NUMBER>, or REQ-<NUMBER> in a project without modules.

Domain fact: something true whether or not this project exists. "A test item in the test manager is linked to the tracker item of the requirement it verifies" is a fact; nobody on the project chose it and no project test can fail it. Prefix FACT-.

Constraint: a limit imposed from outside that design cannot trade away: a regulation, a company procedure, or a platform behaviour. "Approval cannot be performed by a machine account" is a constraint. Prefix CON-.

Decision: a choice made among options, recorded with what the options cost and what the choice commits the project to. Choosing not to build something is a decision. Prefix DEC-.

The reviewed summary or held document a record came from is a source (Sources). Records cite it; it is never a record itself.

docs.title: Verbs
docs.text:
RFC 2119 as clarified by RFC 8174: only the uppercase form is binding, so an ordinary "must" or "should" in prose carries no weight.

Word Means MUST, MUST NOT A requirement. Binding. The only form a requirement record is written in SHOULD, MAY Not used in a record. A statement in this form is not a requirement (no modal verb) A statement of fact, about the world or about something outside the project's control

"Results imported into the test manager sometimes arrive without a build identifier" has no modal verb, so it is a domain fact. "VOGON MUST reject a result import with no build identifier" is the requirement beside it.

VOGON writes MUST, not "shall". ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 uses "shall"; GAMP 5, EU Annex 11 and 21 CFR Part 11 prescribe no modal verb, only that a requirement be unambiguous, testable, uniquely identified and traceable.

docs.title: Systems
docs.text: Term What it is Tracker The issue tracker holding work items such as requirements, with their priority and assignee. Where the project approves in the tracker, it also holds the approvals. VOGON 0.1 is tested with Jira Test manager The system holding test cases, test runs and results, which produces the coverage and traceability reports. VOGON 0.1 is tested with Xray. A project may have none Repository host The service holding the git repository and reviewing changes before they merge. VOGON 0.1 is tested with GitHub Document system The controlled document management system where the validation package is filed and signed

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Term What it is Acceptance criteria The part of a requirement that states what must be tested. Approved with the requirement Test A pytest function. Its req marker names the requirements it verifies. A test with a req marker is the test case for those requirements Test procedure A document, not code: numbered steps in prose, each with its expected result, with an id and linked to its requirement. Projects call it a test script, test protocol or manual test case; VOGON says test procedure, because "script" reads as code. Written and approved as tests.md states

docs.title: Who signs what
docs.text:
A validated system's documents are signed by roles named in the validation plan, as the project process files state them. The requirement approver is defined in src/vogon/references/lifecycle.md "Requirement approver". vogon.yaml lists the people who hold each role, so records and generated documents name the role and never the person. The roles below are common ones; a project uses the roles its plan names.

Role What this person normally does Formal role in validation Product Owner One named person who owns the backlog and decides what gets built next Approves the requirements where requirements.md names this role or no role, with vogon:approve or in the tracker. vogon.yaml lists the holders under product_owner Test Lead One of the engineers, named to review the test procedures Approves the test procedures and test documents the validation plan assigns to this role, as tests.md and documents.md state

docs.title: Where these terms come from
docs.text:
• ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018, the requirements engineering standard: requirement attributes (identifier, statement, rationale, source, verification method, status), the characteristics a well-formed requirement has, and constraint as a defined term. Its "shall" convention is not followed here.
  • RFC 2119 and RFC 8174: MUST, SHOULD and MAY, and the rule that only the uppercase forms are binding.
  • ISPE GAMP 5, Second Edition (2022): user requirement, the requirements traceability matrix, and per-requirement risk classification.
  • The architecture decision record is a convention from a 2011 post by Michael Nygard, not a standard.
  • One file per record, named by id, grouped by id prefix follows Doorstop, the closest existing tool for keeping requirements in git.
  • domain fact is local to this project. The nearest standard equivalents are 29148's assumptions and dependencies and the business-analysis term domain knowledge, and neither names what these files hold.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
Documentation for people operating VOGON: installing it, running it, and producing the evidence your quality unit will ask for.

  • Installation

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: VOGON is a Claude Code plugin. It is installed into Claude Code, and it creates its records and configuration in the host project when it is set up. Nothing from the plugin is copied into the host project.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Claude Code.
  • Git, for the repository the records live in.
  • uv, which runs VOGON's scripts.
  • Python 3.11 or later, which uv installs if it is missing.
  • An MCP server connected to Claude Code for each system role the project uses: tracker (for example Jira or GitHub Issues), test manager (for example Xray), document system, repository host (for example GitHub), meetings (for example Teams or Google Meet), mail (for example Outlook or Gmail) and chat (for example Teams or Slack). A role with no server is not used.
  • In the tracker and the test manager, every transition that records an approval asks the approver for their own credentials.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
Open Claude Code in the host project's repository and run:

/plugin marketplace add pcingola/vogon --scope project
/plugin install vogon@vogon --scope project

Both commands take --scope project. Without it they default to user scope, which enables VOGON in every project the user opens. With it they write the marketplace and the plugin into the host project's .claude/settings.json, and nothing into the user's settings:

{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "vogon": {"source": {"source": "github", "repo": "pcingola/vogon"}}
  },
  "enabledPlugins": {"vogon@vogon": true}
}

Commit that file. Claude Code then offers to install the plugin to every developer who opens the project, and VOGON is active in no other project. Claude Code keeps the downloaded plugin files in a cache under ~/.claude/plugins/; the cache does not enable the plugin anywhere.

docs.title: Set up a host project
docs.text: Ask Claude Code to set up VOGON. It runs the vogon:init skill. Architecture describes what setup does.
